newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cathay income struggles to match capacity.
newsitem.headline: Cathay income struggles to match capacity.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways "struggled to increase revenue in line with capacity" during March in the face of tough targets and a depressed Japanese market, Willy Boulter, general manager, sales distribution and revenue management said.
Writing in Cathay's in-house newspaper, he said overall revenue growth of 4.8 percent was achieved, six percent down on the month's target.

"Hong Kong put in a strong performance with 21 percent growth, missing its target by a whisker. Taiwan recovered and beat target by nearly eight per cent. Japan remained difficult with fewer passengers and a weaker yen. Korea also has a difficult month," Boulter said.

Other areas on the Cathay network did "extremely well" with the Pacific and south east Asia beating budget convincingly while several European countries showed double digit growth. The U.S. was 12 percent ahead of target and sales were 63 percent up on last year. The Philippines was 5.6 percent ahead of target. South Africa recorded a 50 percent increase on last year's sales, Cathay said.

Malaysia recorded 48 percent growth which was 34 percent above target. Both Kuala Lumpur and Penang set cargo revenue records in March despite continued disruptions at Kuala Lumpur's cargo warehouse, Cathay said. The airline recently began two additional services to Kuala Lumpur.
After a period of weakness, Singapore recorded 10 percent growth over the same month last year. Indonesia grew by 14 per cent and Bahrain beat target by 25 percent.

The British market continued its pre-election boom with 20 percent growth in sales, six percent above target, Cathay said. Germany's market growth increased 10 percent, France also increased by an unspecified amount but missed its target and Italy "finally revived" with nine percent growth.
The Benelux countries and Switzerland saw falling sales on last year and Scandinavia performed better off-line than when connected on-line, Boulter said.
"Futher support to the north Asian routes is needed but south east Asia and the Pacific appear strong. Europe seems set to grow. Yield, as ever, is an issue," Boulter concluded.
